title: Butterfly emerges from stellar demise in planetary nebula NGC 6302
caption: The Butterfly Nebula, NGC 6302, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
celestial: Bug Nebula, Butterfly Nebula, NGC 6302 · constellation Scorpius · about 4000 light-years away (source figure)
credit: NASA, ESA and the Hubble SM4 ERO Team

recognition.text: Ranked #20 on ESA/Hubble’s published “Top 100 Images” list (an institutional selection, not an audience score).

story: Two broad, glowing wings spread from a dark band that pinches the middle, their outer edges tinged with red and their inner parts laced with white. It looks like a delicate butterfly, but NGC 6302, a planetary nebula roughly 3800 light-years away in Scorpius, is anything but calm.

The wings are gas heated to nearly 20 000 degrees Celsius, racing outward at more than 950 000 kilometers per hour. At the center is a dying star once about five times the Sun's mass. It has shed its outer layers over about 2200 years and now floods them with ultraviolet light, making them glow. Its surface temperature is estimated at over 220 000 degrees Celsius, but the star itself is hidden inside a doughnut of dust, the dark band.
That dusty ring squeezes the outflow into an hourglass shape. Filters tuned to individual elements let astronomers read the gas's temperature, density and makeup.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (2.35 x 2.74 arcminutes) and distance (4000 light years), the frame spans roughly 2.7 × 3.2 light-years. Its light set out about 4,000 years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3 took this in ultraviolet and visible light, using filters that isolate light from oxygen, helium, hydrogen, nitrogen and sulfur. The caption says the reddish edges trace nitrogen and the white regions trace sulfur.
understand.eye: Part of this data is ultraviolet light, which the eye cannot see, and each filter picks out a single chemical element's glow rather than the blended color an eye would register.

behind.people: See full credit: NASA, ESA and the Hubble SM4 ERO Team
behind.exposure: Not published on the source page.
behind.technique: Not stated by the source (single frame, stack, mosaic or panorama unknown).

explore: The red edges come mostly from nitrogen, tracing the coolest gas in view, while white areas glow with sulfur where fast gas crashes into slower material, making shock waves. Finger-like features pointing back at the star may be denser blobs resisting the wind.

The whole butterfly stretches more than two light-years, about half the distance from the Sun to Proxima Centauri. Before this stage, the star swelled into a red giant about 1000 times the Sun's diameter.
alt: A butterfly-shaped nebula with two glowing wings, reddish outer edges and white patches, pinched at the center by a dark band.
